slides.title: Multiplying and Dividing in Scientific Notation
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say the 'today' line and nothing else yet.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.sub: On your own. Four minutes. No notes.
slides.note: Q1 and Q2 are the two halves of today, side by side. Q1 is yesterday's rule, where the power of ten sat still and only the coefficients moved. Q2 is the rule that takes over today, where the power of ten is the thing that moves. Say at the reveal: multiplying is not adding, so nothing has to line up.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Write the product with the parentheses as given, then regroup: coefficients together, powers of ten together. The two laws you already own finish it — multiply the coefficients, and the product of powers law adds the exponents. Say out loud that the powers of ten did not have to match; nothing lines up in a multiplication. Then the state guide's named wrong answer: a student who multiplies the exponents turns 6 × 10⁹ into 6 × 10²⁰. Ask how many zeros each of those has.
OFF: 'Multiply the fronts, add the backs. The powers of ten never have to match when you multiply.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Split the fraction into two fractions: coefficients over coefficients, power over power. Divide the first, subtract the exponents in the second — top minus bottom, in that order. The second line is the one the state guide asks for and the book never does: a quotient that crosses from very large to very small. Subtracting a negative exponent moves the answer up, not down, and 10⁸ ÷ 10⁻⁴ is 10¹² — a trillion, not ten thousand.
OFF: 'Top minus bottom, always in that order. And subtracting a negative goes up.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
The last step is yesterday's last step, unchanged, and it comes up far more often in multiplication than it did in addition: two coefficients under 10 can easily multiply to more than 10. A quotient can go the other way and land under 1. Neither is a finished answer.
OFF: 'Coefficient over 10, point left and exponent up. Coefficient under 1, point right and exponent down. Same repair as yesterday.'

slides.title: Example 1
slides.sub: Multiplying, and the answer needs finishing.
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. The exponents are seven apart, which would be illegal in an addition and is nothing at all here. Ask for the coefficient product before anything else: will 4.5 times 6 be over 10?

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Regroup, multiply, add the exponents, then repair. A board with 27 × 10⁴ has the value right and is not finished; a board with 27 × 10⁻²¹ multiplied the exponents.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Same shape, the other sign on the small exponent. 2.5 · 8 = 20, and 10⁶ · 10⁻² = 10⁴, so 20 × 10⁴ — which is not finished. 2 × 10⁵ is right.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.sub: Multiplication and division in one expression.
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. The state guide's own item. Ask for the plan first — the two on top, then the one underneath — and make the plan the thing that is praised, not the answer.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: The intermediate value is 60 × 10⁶, which is exactly the unfinished form — and it does not have to be repaired yet, because the division is still to come. Repairing at the end is fewer steps and fewer chances to slip.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: A negative exponent inside the product and a division that pushes the answer below 1. 6 · 4 = 24 and 10⁵ · 10⁻³ = 10², then 24 ÷ 8 = 3 and 10² ÷ 10⁴ = 10⁻².

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

A student who writes 'they both got it wrong' has named nothing.
